sections.heading: Girls' grammar schools
sections.summary: About 61 state grammar schools, entry at 11, and a folklore about English weighting that the evidence does not support.
body: England has 163 fully selective grammar schools, listed by the 1998 Grammar School Ballots Regulations. Around 61 of them are girls-only, 56 are boys-only, and the rest take both. Those three numbers come from counting that statutory list by hand, so treat them as indicative rather than official: the Department for Education publishes no equivalent breakdown, and the figures circulating on the web mostly trace back to a Wikipedia list.

The 163 figure itself is solid. The National Grammar Schools Association says England has 164, a difference of one that is well within the noise of two sources updating on different days. Northern Ireland has a further 69, which are not part of the English list and follow a different admissions system.

The girls' sector is unusually concentrated. Kent and Medway alone account for 13 of them, and the common pattern is a pair: a town with a boys' grammar and a girls' grammar, the way Tunbridge Wells, Dover, Reading and Plymouth each have one of each. In Kent, every selective school in the Maidstone and Malling planning group is single-sex. That matters when you are checking which papers a sibling sat, because the two schools often share a consortium paper.

sections.heading: Do girls' schools test differently?
sections.summary: In the state sector, no evidence of a systematic difference. In the independent sector, yes, and it is a difference of shape rather than content.
body: You will hear it said constantly: girls' grammar schools weigh English and verbal reasoning far more heavily than boys' schools do. The number behind it is real. Some consortia weight English and verbal reasoning together at 50%, with maths at 25% and non-verbal reasoning at 25%. But those are consortium papers serving both sexes, and where the same paper is sat by a girls' school and a boys' school the weighting is identical for both. Warwickshire runs one GL paper across six grammars, three of them girls', and all six sit the same thing. Buckinghamshire reports the same 50/25/25 split for its girls' schools as for its boys'.

So the honest answer is that we found no authoritative source showing a systematic gender difference in the state sector, in either direction. The folklore is probably a reasonable generalisation from particular local consortia, read as a national rule.

The difference that is real, and well documented, is in the independent girls' sector. Cheltenham Ladies' College does not run a multiple-choice paper at all. Its assessment day combines group discussions and activities with written and adaptive online tests in maths, English and verbal reasoning, and the decision uses the current head teacher's reference as well as the day itself. Non-verbal reasoning is absent. That is a different shape of process, not a different weighting, and it is the kind of thing a family considering an independent girls' school needs to know several years ahead.

body: If your child is going up for September 2027, the registration deadlines above have mostly passed. That is worth knowing early rather than late, because the window between registration and the test is the one part of this a parent can actually control.

For the independent route the shape is different again. ISEB Common Entrance at 11+ runs two sessions a year, in November and January, with most children sitting the January one, and the papers are English, mathematics and science. It costs 130 pounds, or 50 if your child is moving up from the school's own prep school. ISEB's Common Pre-Tests are a different thing: four adaptive online tests covering the same four subjects in about two hours fifteen minutes, sat once in a window running from 1 September 2026 to late May 2027, and the result is shared, so every school that accepts it sees the same score without your child sitting it twice.

sections.heading: What the schools say about preparation
sections.summary: The published advice from the exam providers and the schools, quoted rather than paraphrased.
body: This is the part that surprises parents, so it is worth quoting rather than summarising. Cambridge describes its assessments as designed so that children can demonstrate what they are capable of without coaching and excessive preparation. Lancaster Girls' Grammar School, which sets its own FSCE test covering English and maths, says the test is built to remove any need for tutoring, that nothing in it should surprise or intimidate a child, and that no tutor or parent will have knowledge of the test that others lack.

GL draws the same line between two of its own products. Its free familiarisation papers aim for general familiarity with the style of test. Its paid practice papers offer comprehensive preparation. Only one of those is a claim that practice will help you, and it is the one you pay for.

The preparation advice published by a girls' grammar school is worth reading in full, because it is not what most families expect: work well at primary school with maximum attendance, read widely and deeply, keep maths fluent through real day-to-day problems, have imaginative and critical discussions at the dinner table, and focus on calmness and confidence rather than pressure. Notice what is absent. No mention of past papers, of drilling, or of a target number of questions a week.
points: Cambridge: assessments let children show their potential without coaching and excessive preparation.
Lancaster Girls' Grammar: the test is designed so no tutor has an advantage.
GL: free papers are for familiarity with the format; only the paid papers claim preparation value.
